implementation_notes: Kotlin's standard library ships the lazy form directly: Sequence<T> produces elements while iterating instead of holding them, and multistep processing is executed lazily - computation happens only when the result of the whole chain is requested - so filter/map/take do not build the result of each intermediate step. Sequences offer the same operators as Iterable, so converting is one asSequence() call (and toList()/toSet() to come back), with sequence {} and generateSequence as lazy sources. The documentation is explicit that the lazy nature adds overhead, so Iterable (eager) remains the better choice for small collections or simple computations.
code_sketch:
val total = people.asSequence()
    .filter { it.age > 18 }        // no intermediate List
    .map { it.score }
    .take(100)
    .sum()
pitfalls: Sequences are single-pass: a sequence backed by an iterator (or one returned from a function closing over mutable state) re-reads that state on each traversal and yields nothing on a second pass.
Each sequence operator is an extension lambda, so every element pays one call per stage; for short chains over small collections the eager Iterable version is faster (documented).
Materializing mid-chain (toList/toSet inside the pipeline) reinstates exactly the intermediate collection the sequence avoided; keep those calls at the boundary.
